_doc: Single source for SD-96's technology choices. Read by video/src/stack.py, which feeds the 5.1 technology slides, the stack table, the drill interlude, the fix-slide 'Rejected' lines and the C4 technology labels (video/diagrams.py), and rewrites the marked regions of the booklet (Stage 5) and OUTLINE.md. Edit here, then run video/src/stack.py sync (build-video.sh and build-sd-booklet.sh do it). A drill is [probe, the answer for the booklet, the short form for the slide]. Text is Markdown-lite: `code` and **bold** only. The narration stays hand-written in video/src/ch4_5.py; the reveal check fails if a slide gains or loses a row the narration does not cover.

cdn: Surrogate-key purge; 60 s for hot links.

stack.heading: Link store: PostgreSQL, sharded by code
stack.title: PostgreSQL, sharded by code, a primary per region's slice
stack.why: Primary key on the code is the unique constraint; one insert wins, the other gets no row back. 6 TB is boring for it; we know how it fails.
stack.how: `link(code char(7) PRIMARY KEY, …)`. A code maps to a shard by hash. Each region is the primary for the links it creates (its slice of the ID space) and holds asynchronous replicas of the others. Each primary has a synchronous standby in another zone. `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (code) DO NOTHING RETURNING code`.
stack.detail: The full row is `(code, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at, status)`. No row back means the code was taken: a `409` for an alias. The idempotency row is written in the same transaction. A custom alias has no ID, so it belongs to no region's slice: its home region is fixed by a hash of the alias, and an alias create is forwarded there (one cross-region hop, for aliases only).
rejected: Cassandra / ScyllaDB

Fits the reads well. But uniqueness needs a lightweight transaction (`IF NOT EXISTS`), a Paxos round per insert, and its multi-region serial modes are easy to get wrong. Its strength, leaderless writes everywhere, buys us nothing at 400 writes a second.
DynamoDB

A conditional put is exactly the constraint, in one region. Global tables resolve concurrent writes by last writer wins, so an alias created in two regions at once could succeed twice. Cloud lock-in too.
One big PostgreSQL
Writes fit. 18 TB with replicas on one primary, one failure domain, and vacuum on a 12-billion-row table: no.
summary: PK is the uniqueness authority; no last-writer-wins across regions
drill: Two regions accept the same alias in the same second. Which write wins, and where is that decided?

Neither region decides alone. An alias has a home region fixed by a hash of the alias; both creates are forwarded to that one primary, and the primary key rejects the second with a 409. The trap is answering 'last writer wins'.
the alias's home region, chosen by hash; the primary key rejects the second

stack.heading: Range allocator: etcd
stack.title: etcd: a compare-and-set on a Raft log
stack.pick: etcd, 3 nodes per region across zones
stack.why: Linearizable compare-and-set by revision; survives one node; tiny load (0.4 leases a second). Often already run for Kubernetes.
stack.how: Key `/alloc/{region}/next`. A lease is one transaction: `If(ModRevision(next) == r) Then(Put(next, n + 1000)) Else(Get(next))`. Committed when a majority of the Raft group has it. No expiring lock, so no clock assumption and no fencing token: a crashed server just leaves a gap.
stack.figure: ![Mechanism M1 at protocol level: two servers race; the revision decides; the log commits on a majority.](diagrams/video-seq-th-lease.pdf){width=95%}
rejected: ZooKeeper
The same guarantee (a conditional `setData` on the znode version, replicated by ZAB). An honest equal; rejected only for running a JVM ensemble for this alone.
Redis `INCRBY`
Fast, but replication is asynchronous: after a failover the new primary may not have seen the last `INCRBY` and hands out the same range twice. That breaks S1 silently.
Cassandra counter or LWT
Counters cannot compare-and-set; an LWT works but ties create to the busiest store.
A PostgreSQL sequence (`INCREMENT 1000`)
Durable and simple, a defensible choice. Rejected because creates would then depend on one link-store shard's fail-over.
summary: linearizable CAS; async replication can reissue a range
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 2 §2.11 (leases and fencing) and part 3 (consensus, Raft)
drill: The etcd leader dies mid-lease. Can two servers end up holding the same thousand IDs?
No. The transaction commits only on a majority; a new leader has every committed entry, and an uncommitted one is retried against the new revision. The worst case is a wasted block, a gap.
commit on a majority; a retry against the new revision; a gap, never an overlap

stack.heading: Shared cache: Redis Cluster
stack.title: Redis Cluster, read cache-aside, a replica per shard
stack.pick: Redis Cluster, 6 primaries + 6 replicas per region
stack.why: A replica per shard, so a shard's loss is a promotion, not a cold slice. LFU eviction. Bought managed.
stack.how: 16,384 hash slots over 6 shards, about 17 GB of the hot set each. Values: URL and status, ~300 B. `SET code v EX 3600±10%` on a miss; the takedown deletes the key directly. `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu`. Replica reads allowed for the hottest slots.
rejected: Memcached
An honest equal: simpler and multi-threaded. Rejected because a node's loss is a cold slice with no replica, which is the stampede of challenge 3, and it has no LFU policy.
Hazelcast

An in-memory data grid with a near cache. Its near cache duplicates our in-process cache, its clients are JVM-first, and its split-brain merge policies solve a problem a cache-aside copy does not have.
No shared cache, store replicas only
Works at 4,000 a second, until a region's redirect servers restart together and every miss lands on the store.
summary: a replica per shard: no cold slice
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 9 (caching: patterns, eviction, stampedes)
drill: A Redis primary fails over. What does a redirect see in the next two seconds?

Requests for that shard's slots time out at 2 ms and fall through to the store, already cut down by the in-process cache and single flight; then the client refreshes its slot map. A takedown delete may hit the old primary, so it is retried until confirmed.
a 2 ms timeout, fall through to the store; a slot-map refresh; the delete retried

stack.heading: In-process cache and single flight: ristretto + singleflight
stack.kicker: Technology · in-process cache and single flight
stack.title: ristretto plus singleflight, inside each redirect server
stack.why: TinyLFU admission keeps the hot set under scans; singleflight coalesces concurrent misses per key. In Java the same pair is Caffeine with an async loading cache.
stack.how: 300,000 entries × ~300 B, about 100 MB per server; lifetime 60 s, 10 s for a not-found. A 404 storm of random codes is admitted only if its frequency beats a resident code's.
stack.figure: ![Mechanisms M4 and M6 at work: three concurrent misses become one lookup; an invalidation, or the lifetime, ends the copy.](diagrams/video-seq-th-cache.pdf){width=95%}
rejected: A plain LRU map
A scan of random codes evicts exactly the hot set: LRU admits everything.
A sidecar cache per host
One more hop and one more process to run, for the job a library does in-process.
No local cache
Every viral click becomes a network call to one Redis shard: challenge 3.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 9 §9.7 (stampede control) and part 6 §6.5 (hot keys)

stack.heading: Click log: Kafka
stack.title: Kafka, partitioned by code, with pre-aggregation at the source
stack.pick: Kafka, 3 brokers per region, replication factor 3
stack.why: A replayable, ordered log per partition: a bug in counting is fixed by replaying a week. Already the company's event backbone in most shops.
stack.how: Topic `clicks`, 32 partitions, keyed by code, 7 days' retention. Today: `acks=1`, a 1 s linger, pre-aggregated per code and country each second. Billed: `acks=all`, an idempotent producer, a disk buffer and an event ID per click.
stack.detail: Pre-aggregation means a viral code is about forty small messages a second, not a hot partition.
rejected: RabbitMQ
A queue: a message is gone once acknowledged. Recounting after a bug needs replay, which a log has and a queue does not.
Kinesis or Pub/Sub
Honest equals if we are on that cloud: buy, not build.
Write straight into the stats store
No buffer against a viral spike, and the redirect's health would depend on the analytics database.
drill: Counting had a bug for three days. How do you fix the numbers?
Replay: reset the counting job's consumer group to three days ago, write corrected counts to a new table, and switch reads over. That is why it is a log, not a queue, and why retention is a week.
reset the consumer group; recount into a new table; why retention is a week

stack.heading: Aggregator and stats store: Flink → ClickHouse
stack.title: A Flink job into ClickHouse
stack.why: Event-time windows with a bound on lateness; exactly-once state with checkpoints; a columnar store that sums on merge and answers by code and day in milliseconds.
stack.how: Keyed by code; 1-minute tumbling windows; 30 s allowed lateness. Billed: de-duplicate by event ID in keyed state kept 24 h. ClickHouse table `ORDER BY (code, day, country)`; rows with the same key are summed in the background.
rejected: Spark Structured Streaming
An honest equal; micro-batches add seconds, which is fine for 'within minutes'.
A nightly batch job
FR3 says minutes, not a day.
Cassandra counters
Not idempotent: a retried increment counts twice. Wrong for anything that may be billed.
A PostgreSQL table
Fine on day one; counts by code, day and country grow into billions of rows, which a columnar store compresses ten times better.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 8 (stream processing: windows, watermarks)

stack.heading: Invalidation and the edge: a Kafka topic and a surrogate-key purge
stack.title: A Kafka topic for servers, a surrogate-key purge for the edge
stack.pick: Kafka topic link-invalidations + CDN purge by surrogate key
stack.why: We already run Kafka; a reconnecting server replays the last minutes instead of silently missing them. The edge purges every copy tagged c/{code} in one call.
stack.how: Each redirect server reads with its own consumer group, from the latest offset, rewinding 5 minutes on start. The takedown service calls the CDN purge API with the surrogate key and retries; the 60 s edge lifetime is the backstop.
stack.detail: The redirect response carries `Surrogate-Key: c/{code}`, so one purge call finds every edge copy.
rejected: Redis Pub/Sub
At most once: a server that was disconnected for a second misses the message and never knows. Acceptable only because the lifetime backstops it, and Kafka's replay costs nothing extra.
Polling the store for changes
40 servers asking every second adds load and a second of latency, and a slow store makes takedowns slower exactly when it hurts.
Purge by URL only
Works, but every edge variant of a URL must be listed; a surrogate key names them all.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 9 (invalidation and the stale-set race)
drill: One redirect server was partitioned for ten minutes during a takedown. Is it still serving the blocked link?

At most for sixty seconds after it lost the event: the in-process lifetime ends the copy, and on reconnecting it rewinds five minutes. Ten minutes is past the rewind, so the lifetime, not the topic, is what guarantees S2 here.
the 60 s lifetime, not the topic, bounds it; the 5-minute rewind

stack.heading: Services: Go on Kubernetes, behind a bought CDN
stack.title: Go services on Kubernetes, behind a bought CDN
stack.pick: Go on Kubernetes, 3 zones per region; a bought CDN
stack.why: Small static binaries, low and predictable pause times for a 20 ms p99, singleflight in the standard extensions. Points of presence are not our business.
stack.how: Redirect pods scale on requests per second; a pod warms its in-process cache from the last hour's top codes before it passes readiness. Rollouts are one zone at a time. The CDN routes cache rules by response header, so only links over a click-rate threshold are edge-cached.
rejected: Java (Caffeine)
An honest equal: Caffeine is the best in-process cache there is. Choose it if the team is a JVM team; tune the collector for the p99.
Serverless functions for the redirect
Cold starts break a 20 ms p99, and per-invocation pricing at 10 billion a month is the most expensive way to run a loop.
Build our own edge
Hundreds of points of presence and anycast routing, for a product whose core is a map lookup.

1: after a fail-over the new primary can hand out a range it already gave away.
2: A hash of the long URL
truncated to seven characters it collides, and one URL would get one code for every owner.
3: they spread the hot key over two nodes, not forty, and every click is still a network hop.
4: A CDN without a purge API
the 60-second edge copy could not be taken back early.
5: at most once: a server disconnected for a second never learns.
6: they remove the row lock but count a retried increment twice.
7: every create would pay a cross-region quorum; right for money, wrong for a 400-a-second link create.
8: one vantage point that sees only the edge, never create-to-redirect or a takedown.
